report:
Yes—offering HIV self-testing (HIVST) as an additional option generally causes more people to test, especially people who might not use facility/community testing. WHO recommended HIVST in 2016 as a safe, accurate, effective way to reach key populations, men and young people, and reiterated it as an added approach to standard services: https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/WHO-CDS-HIV-19.36

The strongest causal evidence comes from randomized trials. A 2021 systematic review of 14 RCTs in general populations found HIVST about doubled testing uptake versus standard HIV testing services, across several delivery models and support tools: https://www.thelancet.com/journals/eclinm/article/PIIS2589-5370(21)00271-6/fulltext

For MSM and trans people, a 2020 meta-analysis found HIVST increased uptake (RR 1.45, 95% CI 1.20–1.75), increased testing frequency, and raised overall positivity yield, without clear increases in social harm or reduced condom use: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7713313/

Important caveat: more testing does not automatically mean better outcomes. Some evidence found linkage to confirmatory testing/care can be poorer after self-testing unless programmes add active follow-up, reminders, counselling, or easy referral pathways: https://www.aidsmap.com/news/feb-2021/hiv-self-testing-increases-uptake-hiv-testing-poorer-linkage-care

Bottom line: add HIVST to increase testing uptake, but pair it with strong linkage support.
